frase_gancho.texto: A king covered in jade to be reborn as the Maize God (Corn God).

puente_narrativo.texto: This mask did not turn up in a display case, but in a secret chamber. Look for the life-size re-creation of that tomb: a stone sarcophagus under a red light.

guion_corto.texto: This jade mask covered the face of Pakal, the most famous king of Palenque, who died in the year 683. It stands about twenty-five centimeters tall and is made of hundreds of pieces of jade, carved one by one and fitted together like a mosaic. The eyes are white shell with obsidian pupils, which is why the gaze seems alive. Notice the slightly open mouth: the upper teeth form the ik sign, the symbol of wind and breath. The long nose that continues the line of the forehead was the ideal of beauty among the Maya nobility. For the Maya, jade was water, young maize, and life. To cover the king with it was to turn him into the Maize God, so that he would be reborn.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine a door that no one opens for more than twelve hundred years. When it finally opened, in 1952, everything inside was still in its place: an enormous sarcophagus, a skeleton covered in red dust and, over its face, this mask.

The archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier had spent years exploring the Temple of the Inscriptions, in Palenque, Chiapas. It is said that he noticed something odd in the floor of the temple: a slab with holes plugged with stone stoppers. Beneath it was a staircase filled with rubble. It took him four years to clear it. On June 15, 1952, he finally reached the crypt, and there was Pakal. They say that, as he entered, the walls of the chamber glistened, covered by a layer of calcium crystals formed over the centuries.

Who was he? Pakal, whose name means “shield,” took the throne of Palenque as a boy of twelve and ruled for more than sixty years. He died very old, around eighty, a remarkable age for his time. Under his rule, Palenque filled with temples, palaces, and inscriptions. To bury him, his family covered his body with cinnabar, a red powder that for the Maya evoked blood and dawn, and surrounded him with necklaces, bracelets, ear ornaments, and rings of jade.

Today we know that this mask is not a faithful portrait of the old man. It is thought to idealize the king: it shows him eternally young, like the Maize God, who dies and is reborn with every harvest. Pakal was not going to the underworld as a mere mortal, but as a seed that would sprout again. It is the same idea as the [Teotihuacán mask](mna_s04_mascara_serpentina) you saw earlier, taken to the extreme.

He did not spend his first years in power alone: Maya history remembers his mother, Lady Sak Kuk, as the one who passed on to him the right to rule. And the jade, moreover, came from far away. It is believed that much of it came from the Motagua Valley, in Guatemala, hundreds of kilometers from Palenque. Remember the jade of the [bat god](mna_s07_mascara_murcielago) from Oaxaca: here it becomes an entire face. Jade was not worked with metal tools, which the Maya did not have: it was worn down with sand, water, and a great deal of patience, and every piece of the mask is the result of hours of work. Hundreds of pieces, carved one by one, were the most valuable gift a king could receive. The mask was restored at the start of this century: it was put back together with the help of the records made in 1952.

To see the place where it was found, you do not need to travel to Palenque. A few steps away, the hall reproduces the burial chamber at full scale, with its sarcophagus under a red light. There you will better understand why a king bid farewell to the world covered in jade, cinnabar, and gods.

Look at this mask one last time. A king who ruled for more than sixty years wanted to make sure his gaze would remain alive. More than thirteen hundred years later, he succeeded.

texto.Dimensions: 0.245 m high x 0.185 m wide x 0.11 m thick
texto.Discovery: June 15, 1952, by Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, in the crypt of the Temple of the Inscriptions

texto.pregunta: Myth: An astronaut travels in his spaceship on the lid of Pakal’s sarcophagus.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is the king falling into the underworld, with the world tree growing behind him: an image of death and rebirth.
